segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This conversation with Glen Gilder took place at his home not far from the Spring Valley Reservoir outside of Troy on December 9th, 1976. His wife Agnes Gilder also took part in the conversation. The interviewer was Sam Schrager. Were they active when you were a kid?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, very… yes, when I was a kid they were. But you know, they're kind of old. You see, we had a good organization in Deary, and they had one here in Troy, but the membership just kept going, going, going, going. In Deary we were down to seven active members. Well, it's not enough. So we argued for two years, and finally we went in with Potlatch. And Troy argued for quite a period, and then they went all to Moscow. So, all the Odd Fellows here in town go to Moscow once in a while, Al Severson and Monty Helm. oh, quite another. Art Fiddler… i don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When did you first get interested in them?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, when I was a kid, I was pretty young. I was all fixed up to join the Odd Fellows along about 19, 19, with another group of young guys. And somehow or other, I got a job clear out of the country and had to go take it, so I didn't get in on that bunch. And then I didn't join until about 1965, probably, before I joined them. And I wouldn't have joined them then, but Carl Lancaster and Henry Jones and Dwight Corey, well, Carl and Henry were to go in with me in that first bunch. And they made up their mind by the guy that was going to get me in there, and they did it. But it was 1920 to 1965 before I did it. Now, those fellows had been in the lodge all that time. I've seen one of the last papers where Eunice Jones was given a 50-year pin at Potlatch… well, Edna had more years than that in it. I'll bet you that Edna-

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Butterfield?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Mm-hmm… i'll bet you that they joined along before the team got it. They joined that lodge in- Well, did it say in that paper? I don't think it did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it a big, a major thing in the early years? Was it a really big work position?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: You bet it was. You bet.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did it compare to, like, the Grange?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It had much more percentage. It bought them much more percentage than the Grange does. Take a little place like Princeton. And back during the early times, that Grange had around 70 members. And it dwindled down, down, down, and they went in with Potlatch… Potlatch… mm-hmm… Princeton went to Potlatch.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In the Grange?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, in the Odd Fellows. Odd Fellows. You're talking about-… yeah, it was strong. Not only here, but all over the United States. It had tremendous membership. In fact, there was Woodman, and the Redman, and the Masons, and the Odd Fellows. And I think Odd Fellows were- times were the highest of all, but I think there was times when they were- for long periods when they were second. The Redman I think have completely quit. The Woodman of the world have- I think have quit. And the Odd Fellows, then, are probably in third place, second or third place.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, with the Odd Fellows, that was a lot bigger than the Grange at the time, wasn't it, when you were growing up? A bigger- I mean, around here. I think so.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, the Grange was pretty popular, too. Well, a big percentage of the Odd Fellows were Grangers. Same then as they are now, here in Troy. There's Alfred and Art, Monty. They're all Odd Fellows.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There's a lot of overlap between the two... Well, what's the difference between- is there much difference between the Odd Fellows and, like, the Masons as a group?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: They have different policies. I don't know very little about the Masons, but their purposes have always been pretty parallel, I believe. They have fellowship to benefit everybody involved in it. All that good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old were you, Glen, when you started working out… you were here?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, I don't know, about twelve.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the first work that you did out?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, driving horses for somebody, I suppose. Yeah, I think that's it. I don't know. It was just natural for me to drive horses, be around horses, as anything could be. When I first started hauling wheat from Kennedy Ford into Palouse for my uncle and granddad, I couldn't more lift a sack of wheat than I could fly. Nobody else had to load me and unload me. But I could drive the horses, four of them. I didn't take a back seat there from any of the big fellas either. Then from there I went to drive in, oh, one of the first jobs I had to drive in a greater team on a highway greater from Harvard to the hoodoos. Old Duff used to come get me every spring and take me up with him. I'd step up two weeks and we'd fix all the culverts and clean out the ditches and grade the roads. I'd go home and have about, oh, maybe fifty dollars. I didn't make much in them days. I think about two dollars in a half a day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you quit school by that time?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No. If I need to, I'd take a week off. I'd go back and I was going to catch it up, but I don't think I ever did. There was nothing uncommon. If you got a job, go do it. Lots of times we could get a job for driving a team and wagon putting gravel on the road. In the fall of the year we could get a couple of weeks' worth. All we had to do was drive a team back and forth. Somebody else loaded us and then somebody helped us unload the dump boards. That's what I would sooner do. That's what I did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You would sooner do than sit in the classroom?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No. If I was sitting in the classroom, I don't know for sure, but I think I must have spent a lot of my time looking out the window. I don't know, but I think I must have.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it true for you that, now I've heard a couple of people say that to do a man's work is really what they wanted to do as a boy. To be able to do a man's work was what they were looking forward to. Would you say that was true for you?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, it was true. To compete with a man seemed to be the height of our ambition. We were lucky and could keep up with him. We thought we were pretty big. If we could catch one that was a little older or a little awkward and could surpass him or something, then we had to swell head. We was always saying. Take two kids out shocking hay with a pitchfork. They'd race from morning till night, try to get that road done quicker than the other guy. I worked one year for Lindsay. He had me shocking and she'd come out in the field pretty early in the morning after she got housework done. Her and I would race till noon. She'd go and get dinner after about dishes done and all that. She'd be right back out there in Dogland if we didn't race then until she had to go milk. We'd go out and make fun of each other like a couple of kids.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: She was forty-five years older than I was, about seventeen or eighteen. She worked awful hard, seriously. They made it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it pretty common to do what she did for the women, to get out and work?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It was really common the women got out and helped. Sometimes they eliminated the hired men altogether. Many, many, many of them. They could drive horses as good as a man. You bet the wives and daughters they were right out in the field.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: They didn't live so long. They didn't live so long?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I don't know, Amelia's still going good… amelia who… lindsay. She wasn't the last time I saw her, about fifteen years ago. She wasn't going real good, but then she's still going.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you figure that that was pretty rough on women to do that then? Agnes, is that what you think?

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yes, I do… they didn't get over it so good. Nothing looked like it, but they didn't. She worked her head off, that's for sure, and paid for it.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Her big trouble is she got off so heavily. She was way overweight.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And then she was still working?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, no while she was still working she was right. Oh, right on to a good working order, I think. I think she waited on 130, 40, 50, somewhere around there, but now she's over 200. Well, I didn't know her when she was younger. When she was about, well her kids were about five or six years old. She had a hard girl life too, she helped and then went out and did. She did. After they got, well started and established, she had Genevieve and Neom and some of them, but for a number of years she just didn't. But if she wasn't alone in that, all the neighbors, the Hansons, the Hoggins, and all those people that were close to them, it was all the same thing, the Gregorys.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it just necessity that dictated it, that that's what a woman would do, or was it more trying to get ahead?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, it was quite a bit of a necessity because times weren't a great deal better than they are in this day and age. You might have had less money, but it became just as hard as it did in the last few years. Well, they had to sell a couple of hogs or a calf or something to pay us fellows our wages for the help they got in harvest and haying. Money was hard to get, but it wasn't easy. And they all were starting. They had places to pay for and outfits to pay for and learning to make. That's one thing though, in those days young men and women got a better start than they have any chance of having now. Oh yeah. Of course they were. They're up to 150 ,000 now, maybe 15 ,000. They've taken care of the whole thing, the deal in those days, but it's pretty hard to get, just saying.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It's funny that there's a lot less opportunity now than there used to be. I think there'd be a way you could still compete.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, up to this last year it has been possible, but boy I don't think anybody can get ahead now. Well, I... no. They're just awful lucky to be able to come out even.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: What year?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Back before 1928. If a man had $100 he could start farming in a good shape.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you serious? $100?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: We rented 80 acres and I had a harvest, what I'd made and harvested. And Harold had an equal amount and we bought a Ford car with it. And we went to work in the mill. Every time we'd get a paycheck we'd buy a horse or a calf or a harness or a plow or some damn thing. And we got started. We didn't have any cash, we just... every time we could make a dollar... We just applied it to some little thing that'd probably grow. And most of it did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You didn't have to spend much of that money just to live on at that time?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh no, eggs and beans and spuds were cheap. That's about all we knew how to cook. We'd match them before we married.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now is this your own place that you had at the time?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, we rented 80 acres from my grandmother. Got a start there. We did pretty good for 27, 28 and 29. Made some pretty good headway. And then the depression came and we went the other way.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the deal with your grandmother? Was it a certain amount of money you paid or what?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, we gave her $125 a year for that place. She was tickled the death to give it to us… just for rent.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you grow a crop on it?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, you bet. Good one. Our first crop on that place... 40 acres... I think it was only about 28 acres a week, but it made 42 bushels. And we got $2 .15 a bushel. And that was making darn good money. Had two years of that and then the depression hit and wheat was worth $0 .25 a bushel. That's a different story. That wouldn't pay for... ...any part of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the stock that you say you were buying? Were you raising them up then? You said you'd buy a pig or a calf?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yes, we did. We'd buy little pigs, little calves. And they grow and... Actually, that's all the gain we made is about what they grew, but... ...even that was pretty good for that time. Oh... It's a different world. I don't know. I asked a lady in Wyoming last... What would cost to start ranching over there? And she told me... ...it would cost a million dollars. If they could get ahold of the lease... ...if they could get ahold of the land that is the homestead and the home ranch... ...and then to get ahold of a lease and keep it up... ...keep up their water rights... ...and stock enough to stock it... ...and the machinery enough to take care of it... ...that that's about what it would cost. Well, a young guy can't start unless you got a dad or granddad... ...with money to put him on the place.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: And it's the same in wheat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It doesn't sound like it was easy, though, even in the 20s when you were doing it. I mean, it wasn't a... It certainly seemed like an easy haul to build up.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It wasn't, but... ...we were talking it over before we leased this place... ...and said if we could get a job in the middle, which we thought we could... ...that was eight hours. But it wouldn't hurt us to go home and do chores after those eight hours... ...any more than it would if we drove a team on a plow all day... ...and then went in and done chores in the same way. No, it wasn't easy. It was long hours. And hard work. It could have been a lot of going without, but we were young... ...and didn't know enough to go without anything. We wanted something like that. We went and done it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What would you...give me a for instance of what you'd do instead of that you couldn't go without?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, go take our girl to the show or... ...or go to a dance. It was probably a couple of dollars. And now, it would cost you $25. We didn't go without because we didn't... They didn't have things like they've got them now. The only thing you could do is go to a show or go to a dance... ...or go to a party in somebody's house. That's all it was. A couple of dollars was plenty for a weekend. But that couple of dollars was so big then... ...that I don't know whether the 25 is any bigger now than that was. I don't know. I don't think so.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you really holding down two jobs at once when you were doing that?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yes, that's exactly right. I had some plowing to do after I got home from the mill at 3 o 'clock if I was on the day shift. I'd go out and plow till 6 or 7. And that's the way I got all the work done. After work, do it. It was a small place. By figuring and scheming, taking turns... ...and another thing we could do, we had fairly good horses. We could... ...when I traded with my uncle... ...he'd put my crop in and then take my horses over to his place for the summer. Well, all I had to do as far as putting in my crop then was to buy the seed. And we did that one year. I did the work, but I don't think I did the thinking.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Scheming work and did a lot of thinking. Why didn't you do the thinking, Glen? I don't know what you mean. You mean you didn't think about it enough… oh..… i mean, did you?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, you had to... I don't know. You had to scheme and plan... ...and wonder, how the devil are you going to make it? What are you going to do to make this come out right? What are you going to do to make that come out right? I didn't always hit it right. I missed it a few times. But then... ...that's what I mean by thinking. Man... I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there real choices that you had to make? I mean, you could have gone two or three different ways, I don't think? Well, you could have invested in different ways in the stock...

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: ...or you could have lunged in and hit it, or you could have lunged in and missed it. You know, things then were like they are now. Cattle could be a good price this year, or hogs could be a good price this year. Which they were in those first few years in 27, 8 and 9 way. Hogs were clear up to 13 cents a pound. In 1930 and 31, they were balancing between 2 and 3 cents a pound. I had some of those.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, is that thinking or is that just rolling the dice? I mean, it seems to me like maybe it's a matter of luck.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, just rolling the dice. Anytime that you start farming, you start rolling the dice... ...and you never quit rolling the dice until you quit farming. There isn't any way to quit. Sometimes you can guess ahead, but... ...it's not all head work either. It's an equal amount of pure luck.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did it take you to decide that you'd be better off getting out of that place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, after 3 years it was going darn good, we thought we'd get a little bigger. We did, we got a little bigger. We got a little bigger and put the much produce on the market, I guess. That's why hogs went from 13 cents to 2, because everybody went with us. Well, you're always, always reaching out, trying to boost yourself. Lift yourself up another notch. Sometimes you do it, sometimes you didn't. When wheat was 25 cents a bushel, a sack would hold 2 bushels and a half. And it cost us 30 cents to get the sack. And I think it cost 10 cents a sack to get it thrashed, that's 40 cents. And your seed had cost you around $2 an acre. And your work and your horse work went into it and finished out the crop, but even so, that wasn't enough money to break even. Oh, I don't know. When the depression could come, we did have a few cows to milk and fairly good ones.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: And by working out after my crop was in or during the winter, if I could get work during the winter, I'd take it, but I generally couldn't. If I could cut around three quarters of a cord of wood a day, that was enough to eat on. That's about, for 10 years, that's about what we did. Never had any health or relief or WPA. We didn't have it. We could have got it, I presume. I never tried. I didn't want it. I don't blame the guys that did get it. I think it was more power to them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So really then, it was just holding on, not trying to... The chance of getting ahead during that time wasn't...

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It wasn't. The only way that you could have possibly gone ahead, and some did, they'd acquire more land or more equipment, and then when the prices broke back up to a dollar a bushel, why then, they went right ahead. They had her made. But a guy like myself that didn't have the guts or foresight or whatever it took to do that… didn't do it… when it did come up, we went ahead all right after it came, but we went awful slow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you didn't own the land to start with, right? I mean, you didn't have anybody give you the... No. ...the form to inherit it, or you didn't have the money to buy it when you were a young man, right? I mean, that seems to put you in a different position to start with over some of these guys that had the land.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, we did finally buy that place up at Harvard, and we went... $5 ,000 in debt, didn't we?

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I don't remember. But we lost it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When did you buy it?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: 34 minutes. 35. 34.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I think. I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You'd just been married a pretty short time then, right?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: When you got married. Well, wheat was 30 cents then on the way up. Got up to 60 cents finally and still wasn't enough. Because we were back on payments and we were back on interest, our taxes were kept up, but... You couldn't pay anybody if you owed somebody. You couldn't pay them, so the only thing to do was just not owe them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Go without… how long did you keep that place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Until 1939… yeah, 1939. We had a walking papers and then we came over here. Still hard sledding. It wasn't easy going. I think wheat was 75 cents then. I think cream was what? About... clear up to 15 cents a pound. 11. 11 cents. 11 cents. Well, 11 cents for some of it, but I think it kind of gained a little by the time we got here. Then the war came on. But even that didn't make any difference to us for..… oh, what… it took two or three years for that to affect us here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Very much.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Didn't affect anybody, but the ones that had it already paid for. It took a long time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why? What was their advantage?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Price didn't come up. Price didn't come up for three years after the war. Slow starting, but they did eventually start. During the war all the neighbors around here pulled out and went to work for... ...for war effort.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: A lot of people did that, huh?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, you bet… shultons, Telfries, Davises, Fountains, Basins.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they go to Portland mostly? Seattle? Did they go to Portland mostly?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, no. They went to Bayview. They went to..… every place… any place there was war efforts. One of them went to work up there at the hospital, construction work.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Longview and the ship character and Boeing were the main...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They take their families or just... Most of them, yeah. ...who kept their places, though?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Some of them didn't. Some of them... Most of them didn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Really?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Some of them were so badly indebted, weren't ever going to come out of it anyway, so they just... ...all the way out of here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That was right around here? Right on the creek here?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, right here. Well, Allen's Place, the Muellys, Fountains, and the next one beyond Anna Marie's.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So what did you figure then? Hm? What did you figure then? Were you tempted to go for the war?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, you bet. But I didn't. Oh, I could get a job here and a job there and keep what little headway I had made. I thought I'd make more headway that way than if I did pull out and go into war effort. I believe for once it was right. Because I could get my work done here and go out and go to work for Steel Smiths or Walner or whoever. Pretty good wages. And when harvest or whatever was over, come home and have enough to eat on and keep the kids in some kind of clothes. We did it. I don't know whether it was right or wrong, but... At least we didn't have the expense of moving back and hiring the house, which at that time were just about as bad. You'd find a house any place then as it is now. Well, every one of them that did that spent the rest of their life working for wages. And I did too in a way, but I still had my own incentive here to go ahead and hang on and had my own home. Some place I knew if I got out of a job I could eat and sleep under the rug.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: And it's a long hard haul, but after a while we retired and Uncle Sam went to giving us a little money.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you take some real tight jobs at that time?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, all the way through. Short jobs, long jobs, anything. Worked in the saw mill and come home here and we only had about 75 acres to farm. And the kids were getting big enough that they could help quite a bit. And if I'd come home here Friday night and work till... Well, after we got a tractor and worked till 10 or 11 o 'clock at night. And I'd work all day Saturday and all day Sunday. I'd go back to Wilk at the mill Monday morning with everything pretty well caught up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which mill was this?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, Roush's, Murphy's, Conklin's, Bennett's.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You'd stay there for the week? Or you'd come home every day?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I'd come home every day, yeah. I'd cover through the milk morning and night. After the war and after we got started here and got things kind of leveled off. Things got a lot easier. We got a car and... And could hold a job by going back and forth from here to Moscow. We got pretty good... I always got top wages or just about. And financially it was a lot easier. We did alright.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, during the war, how did you get to work and back? Did you have a car?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, I worked around here close and if I couldn't find some neighbor to ride with, I didn't go. That is a must towards here close. He mostly worked as a field hand there for up till 1950. I think he started to work at the mills.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So Roush's and Bennett's and those places was mostly in the 50s?

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It was before Bennett's time. It was in... Moscow, I don't know. In Portland.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: But Bennett didn't come in there until about 1956.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, when you had the place at... when you got the place at Harvard, were you working at the mill then too?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, I was working in the woods… getting logs… with horses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that contract work you were doing yourself or were you working with other guys?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Both. I generally liked to gyppo contract if I could.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: If it made a dollar extra or two extra, why not?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Most of the time it did. Sometimes it didn't. Mostly the mill company knew just about what the gyppo could make and just about kept it pretty well even. A little less, but they tried to make it look like it could make any loss. Well, they did. They knew exactly what you could make. And the only way you could make that extra dollar was just really tying into it and working. You didn't stop to take a drink. You took a drink on the walk. I think it's probably about the same now. It comes right down to it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I remember hearing that from some guys that... well,… frank Hertzog was one of the people that said that when they first started. gyppo in the early 20s. The men made real good and worked real hard. Cut their own throats.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Company would cut us down if we made too much.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that true in the 30s too?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: That's always true as long as the Potlatch had been in existence.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that a place you had known pretty well when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh yeah. I lived on it. My dad owned it before I did. No, we went there in 1910. And one of the others was on it until 1939.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who did you buy it from?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, I just took over my dad's debts. He couldn't pay them. He was stuck. We thought I could make it, so I tried and didn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He retired then?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, practically he was getting up in years. Had a heart condition. Yeah, he retired. He had to.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did it take you before you could tell you were really going to have difficulty on that flight? She knew right away?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: About 30 minutes I said, Judge. But we never gave up. We fought her right until the last inch.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What made it so hard on that place? Was it the debts that you started with or what?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: You couldn't make all that cheap wheat. You couldn't make a dollar to pay the bill with.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And we'd work out in the woods.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: We could make our groceries and pay our taxes. And most of the expenses. But that wheat just wasn't high enough price to pay that bill. You just wouldn't pay it. Well, then you decided that would be a crop. By the time you thought you were going to make something, all this stuff was coming. Well, we lost two crops from Frost and one from Rust. But this was on a federal land bank contract and they had no sympathy for us. You just, you'll have to control your weather better. Oh, I don't know why a man farmed or I don't know why he done anything. They should have had brains enough to work like they do now. Just go on welfare.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it just the idea of being independent… independent. Right.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Fighting to get that few dollars ahead that would put you so that you didn't have to. In fact, there wasn't any jobs in the mill to shut down. During the Depression, they had, they had, their coblights, they had, um, Said they were out of order or something about the time just before it, that October date, whatever it was. Said they were out of order and we didn't have to shut down for a while. They never shut, or never started up again for, They were geared, I don't know how long it was. It was a little over six years that they was not operating enough to keep people employed. Had some, oh, the mill, or what do you call that, uh, we had, heh, planer mill was going part of the town and that was all. The main part of the mill didn't start up till after, just about the time the war started, the way I remember it. They started operating a little bit in 36, I think.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah. So that was the condition in 34, it was already that way.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: That it was… one guy saw Glen on the street and one of the head ... there said, what we need is a good war. And he finally got it and, That was one of the officials for Potlatch. And he was so right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Doesn't really seem like, like a very dependable answer, does it? I mean you can't just go on and have a good war every 20 years and bail you out.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, it took that to start the economy back to where working man could live a decent life.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Have you been by the outskirts of Potlatch from the white to the town? When we came in, when I first came in 1990, that field there was half full of lumber. Just, I don't know what, but he was sitting out there drying. It was out there drying on 80 acres of it. Well, it wasn't quite 80 acres. Yes, it was, but it didn't tire her.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Ah, couldn't keep waiting until, uh, the,… okay, well.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How much clear land was there on, on your father's place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, right close to 100 acres.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you feel that under, that under favorable circumstances?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: If they'd left us alone for two years, we had her made. We had her made if they'd left us alone for two more years. No question in my mind about it because we had two rough years here, but we had all the expense of moving here and building this place up. And then in two years, we went right ahead from that day on. Yes, if I could have stayed there for two more years, I'd have been wealthy… no fooling… because I had my man made up, but I was going to grow hay on every inch of it, and I had wealth of pasture in that range back there. And I would have stayed with livestock. I didn't want grain. I don't like to wheat farm, never did. It always seemed to me to, always unstable. I know we would have made it. The guy that took over did make it. He had help from everybody in the family too. Well, he made it working.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: We.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: He borrowed $500 to buy that place...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Hi, how are you?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: And when we got through selling, what we had to sell in order to get off the place,… we had this, I think, just $1 ,000. And that was sheep, was the main part of it, but there was about 25 head of cattle. A couple of horses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You had $1 ,000 that you got out of it when you left?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: We come over here with our outfit and $1 ,000, yeah. But that was all of it made by that little stuff growing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How come, I mean, how much debt did you have then? Did they?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: We had about, we was behind, dug on there $3 ,000. Now, if we had sold what we sold to get out of there, well, we would have put ourselves in a pretty good position. But they didn't give us that opportunity. They sold that place in Hayden. Out of a blue sky. I had no idea they were going to sell it. But my contract was behind. There was nothing I could do about that part of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How are you doing… okay… they didn't come to you and really give you the opportunity?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: To deal with it?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: They had offered me all kinds of things and all kinds of deals in advance of that, but they never offered me anything. Pay it up and you're a good boy. Pay it up or you're a bad boy.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So then they turned around and gave this other guy. A pretty good break in the place.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yes, they did. They give them better break than they ever give me… much bigger… now, we were coming all right. We bought a bunch of sheep that followed before. About 75 head. Give a dollar and a half piece for them. When I sold them in the fall of 1939, I got $3 .50 for the old ones. And I got around $6 a piece for the lambs and most of them had twins. Well, give me $12 for the lambs and the $2 profit on the ewes. And that's the sheep were there. If I had had another year, hell, I'd have paid them up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who was it that had the mortgage on the place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: The Federal Land Bank.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That just sounds crazy. Unfair.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It was unfair… but I had some horses. I had six darn good horses and I had around 20 head of cattle. Young, old and indifferent. And they wanted a mortgage on them. And I told them the mortgage on the place is all I can handle. It's all the place is worth. And I refused to give them a mortgage on my stock and outfit. And that made this commissioner mad. Because they told him to come and get it and I wouldn't give it to him. So, he was mad and he thought he'd fix me so I'd be a good boy next time. Well, I'm not as bitter as I sound. I think it all was just things that had to be. I'm to blame for as many of the wrongs as I am for the rights. And I know it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of strikes me is the fact that you didn't turn around after having been given such a tough time on that place and start right up again. You know, come right back at it from another place.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, that's what makes me think so damn sure that if I had had the time there, just a reasonable little bit more time, I'd have had her made. Because I come here on a darn smaller place and it was completely run down. And I come out of it. I don't know what would be the answer. I've always thought that I had her made there if it left me alone and made good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, between 34 and 39, did you have a much bigger mortgage in 39 than in 34 on the place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, I think we just almost kept even. But there'd be, yes, I think there was added on, I think it was $600 or $700 interest. That's what they were screaming about. Well, that's just the case. The Federal Land Bank had to have their income or they couldn't stay in business.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were they satisfied if you paid off the interest or did they want?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, I think if I had paid off all the interest, I believe they would have been satisfied. But they were going to get that mortgage to cover my back interest. I just refused to give it to them. Because if I had to move, I was going to keep something to move with. I wasn't going to just walk away with my pocket full. And I wouldn't give in. Well, they broke me sucking eggs.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But I mean, it didn't really discourage you from the idea that you could make it on a farm. Because you moved down here right away from there, right?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I mean, you didn't give up for five, ten years. No, I didn't give up for a darn minute because I wanted to farm and I knew that a man had some independence. I knew that he could gain a little bit, not very much, always, but a little bit. But I had a family and I had to have a house over them. I had to have food for them. And I'd seen the guys in town. When they got out of a job, they were stuck. And the guy out in the country wasn't quite stuck. He was in hard shape, but he wasn't stuck. He could eat and he had a place to sleep that was dry. And there wasn't any great deal of fear of somebody going to boast him out of it. Because believe me, when we come here, I kept them payments up. If it had to sacrifice a few clothes or an automobile or maybe some food, by gosh, we kept them up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Having a bunch of kids really made a big difference, didn't it? I mean, in terms of what you had to put out. Sure.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: You bet it did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old were you when you were born? Oh, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I had a good friend that was single, same age practically. He stayed single all of his life. And he told me a couple of years before he died that he had a half million dollars. And I told him I had darn near half a hundred, but I wouldn't trade places with him. Yeah, our family was obligation men, the same as it is now. It was no different. It took just about all you could make to keep them going. I was just lucky. Mine did finally grow up. I heard a man say along around 1914, I was about 14 or 15 year old kid, that a man never could make any money until after his family was grown up and gone. I thought it was kind of a funny statement, but you know, it sure as heck proved right… you couldn't… then you can't now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Funny. You know, just to think about it, it doesn't seem that kids ought to require that much besides food to eat, which you could grow a lot of yourself and...

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: They helped.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about clothes?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, food and clothes, but then, you know, through most of that time wages were from a dollar to three dollars a day. And milk or cream by the pound, butterfat, was around, oh, it did finally get up to 15, 20 cents, but... It only just barely... Well, it bought most of the groceries, probably not quite all. But... No, I just... just... just kind of a hard time to live. I should have been born earlier or later if I wanted it easy.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Easy earlier, you think?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, I don't know. Yeah. I don't know what to think.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I... I don't know.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: A man don't know what he'd do under a little bit different conditions. Don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What made you come over to this area to look for a place to move to?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, I'd heard that was less frost hazard and it was good dirt and there was quite a bit of land for sale here, which there wasn't every place. And land was cheaper around here for some reason or other than it was on the Palouse River. I wanted to get away from frost. There's a little frost here over there on here. I never have lost a crop from frost here in the 40 years, but I lost two over there and four. This is good dirt. There's some tremendous crops of grain and hay around here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was that frost like over there? When would it hit?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, in order to hurt the wheat just when it was in bloom, you have to hit it in July. Well, wheat, you have to hit it about 10th of July and that's what it done. I had a contract on 40 acres of peas and I got them in about the 20th of May and around the 20th of June we got a frost and just positively killed them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I had a contract with Spokane Seed Company and I called them up and told them what had happened and they said, well, there's nothing you can do about the weather, is there?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: They just forgot it and wiped it off.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So with hay there's no such problem, right? You don't have to worry about it.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It's a little bit. Well, you never know really about those. Sometimes you do charge for it sometimes. It's quite how the contacts work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I was thinking that growing hay would be, instead of a crop, would be a lot less likely for it to get ruined, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No. No, hay is more resistant. Sometimes it gets spoiled entirely.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you attracted to this place as soon as you saw it?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I made up my mind that we were going to have two things, three things. I think you're darned how small it was. There being no more renting, it was going to be mine if I went on to it. It had to have water and a road and it had all three of them. So we bought it. We looked all over the country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: We looked round and round here for how long? For a solid year?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I don't know. We did it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think of the place when you saw that? Did it look good to you?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: I'd rather write letters and he also sends half a newspaper.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you hear what I asked you? I asked you if the place looked good to you when you first saw it. What was the most important part of this place?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, yeah, it looked alright. It looked as good as the other ones made. Yeah, it was okay. It didn't look like a big enough house for the whole family, but our family was really growing at that time. It didn't look like the last word in anything. There was no buildings, no fences. It needed everything. There wasn't even a great deal of... There was 25 acres of cleared land on it. But we could get a hold of it without putting a big mortgage on it. We sold our cows down too close over there and our sheep too close. So we wound up finally putting a mortgage on this for $1 ,000, but it was in order to get restocked. It was something to work with. And then I started in. I built a barn and fences piece by piece. The barn didn't cost me only the nails. It was in it. Poles and shakes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did you get the lumber from? What lumber?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: There wasn't any in it. There wasn't any in it for several years. And then I traded and got a couple of thousand feet from Roush, but it wasn't sided up or anything for a couple of years. But they did have a roof over the hay and I couldn't go in there and sit down and milk the cows in the dry. There was no floor under them or nothing. But for the first half of the first winter we were here, I milked them out in the snowbank. When I get a big enough roof on that barn to put another cow in there, I thought I was a lucky guy. A runner in there milker. Well, I'll tell you. If I had always had things nice and easy and rosy, I wouldn't have had to get to stay with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the house? Where did you live? There was no house here at all?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, it was a little tiny house. There was one, two, three rooms. There was four rooms. But they were so small that if company came and we were all in there, somebody had to stay outside and push the door shut because they couldn't close it from inside. Oh, it's still such a big house. A little bit of an old shack. But I get shoving them three in a bed while we got by. As soon as we could, we built it back. And they stationed onto it and that took care of the boys. The girls had a good room then. Everything was pretty good until we got squared around and started this. It took us ten years to build this.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Ten years from when you first moved on?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, from the time we started it. Until it was finished like it is now. We would need lumber or we needed this or nails or whatever. We'd get along without them until we could pay cash for them. We didn't have any debt. When the house was done, it was ours. I'd had my debts. So I didn't want any more. It took a long time to do it that way because earn it piecemeal.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What year?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, it didn't cost us a lot of money at that. I logged the logs and then I had a dip hole in here and saw the number for half. And I made it so about all I had to dig down in my pocket for was nails and get it planed until we got it up. And then, of course, it took in wiring and pipe and windows and all that stuff. But we just got a piece at a time and got by.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you wait until it was finished before moving in?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Not exactly. It was all pretty well… pretty well done.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, Glen, you were saying about that you put up the barn when you first came. Besides that, what were the first things you attended to around here?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Well, the fence in the barn was first. That had to be. There just wasn't any. The neighbors on two sides of us were awful good. They helped. And then later on the neighbor on the other side came in and he helped. They didn't share and I did mine. But even so, none of us had money enough to work with. Because there was no wire, there were no posts, there was nothing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So what did you put up the fence with? Who? What? What were the details? What did you use for...

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Oh, how did I get the fence… oh, it wasn't easy. I bought a lot of new wire all I could. I bought it and I'd see somebody out here that had started tractor farming and he'd taken up his fence so I'd trade him something for his old wire and then I'd bring it home and put it up and go out and see if I couldn't trade with another one. I traded a sheep,… see some fellow down at Genesee for a trip load. And I traded a horse for a guy down here on American Ridge for a mile of hog wire fence. And then the Anderson boys gave me enough wire for about a mile of fence for three wires. I was lined up with the darn place. It had around seven miles of fence on it and you could turn a sheep or a hog anyplace on it and he'd stay there. It was tight. And now I've taken it off, it's on my way. I quit the stock.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: At that time, had most farmers around gotten rid of their horses?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, no, there were lots of horses then. But they started right after that to get rid of them. No, but right around here close, no, there wasn't any tractors. Back a mile or two, there was a few. But they started coming in about then. We didn't buy a tractor until about 1952 or three, did we?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were they really a lot better than horses?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: No, those old wheel tractors weren't. No, they weren't better than horses. They were just..… i don't know… we couldn't plow on the hillside with ours. I don't know whether it was us or the tractor, but we never did get so we could do a good job plowing. On the steep hillside, we couldn't go up and down it. That was it. The horses would go round and round or up and down. They didn't care. I was next to the last in the whole area to quit the horses and go to tractor Charlie Barquet down there. Hung on for a year or two after I did. The only way I could see to get a tractor was going down. I didn't want to go down. I'm going to go up.

segments.speaker: Agnes Gilder
segments.words: There's three of them.

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Did you see any advantage at that time to get one? Was it an attractive idea to have one to get rid of the horses? It was ideal for us because we could pull more with it. I took the horses off that. We could hurl and do things like that. But the horses filled in. Both places that were difficult or not effective with the tractor, they were effective with the horses. It was a good system and it would still be good today if we do it. By the time we got our tractor, we had about 60 to 75 acres of hay. That was an awful job for horses. It was terrible on the horses. The mower was really something they could rake and they did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why was the mower hard on them? On the horses? Was it hard on them? No, why was the hay?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: It was heavy and it was hot. They hadn't done very much from the time the spring crop was in until the hay started to give them about a month layoff and they were soft. It made a bad on them. A man felt awful bad about working them that way. When he got that mower, Lloyd mowed 20 acres back there in one day and with the horses it would have taken three. The next day the horses went out and raked it. I still think it would be a good idea to have a good team and use them where they worked the best and forget the tractor. There are so many jobs they can do. The gas is not necessary for them. The rake and haying time are hauling it in. They are actually better than the tractor. They are not faster but they are better. As far as cost goes, there isn't any.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the work steady most of the time? Or would it be sometimes on, sometimes off?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: That's the way it was. I couldn't go back. I didn't have a car or stay away from home on a job. I just had to take hit or miss jobs but that's fine. If I wasn't busy at the job, I was busy here. If you keep the financial end of it up, that wasn't necessary. And it did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could you work as much in the winter or was there a lot of layoff time in the winter?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: To work off the place, the only thing you could do is you might be able to get a job skidding logs someplace. I didn't cut wood and sold it or worked at the buildings. I didn't have to have the wood to eat on. No, it was hit or miss.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you have time to sit around in the winter like now or would you be up and out working every day?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: Yeah, I was working every day at something because stock required it. But I was young and husky and ambitious. I liked to do it. Oh, when the snow would get insufferably deep or it was terribly cold, I could lay off. Yeah, and I did. But it was nice working. I liked to be out of it. I had them plan or something I wanted to accomplish and that's the time to accomplish it. But right now, I couldn't see it as it being tomorrow or any other thing. After we got squared around and got a car with him, I could go back farther, go to Moscow or someplace to work with him. That made quite a difference too. But we didn't have a car. In order to have a car, you had to go in debt. I wasn't interested. I didn't mind the debt if I knew that there was some source to pay it off when the time come, but I'd have that. I'd have my wings trimmed and I never got over it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: About what year was it that you got the car to go?

segments.speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
segments.words: About 1948, I suppose. Got a hundred dollar one. But it went and come back. It's all necessary.

segments.speaker: Unknown Speaker
